tagline: Through mill villages beside the remains of a twenty-year canal
intro: The Blackstone Canal Heritage Highway carries Route 122 through the Blackstone Valley’s mill villages. Between Grafton and the Rhode Island line, the road crosses the Blackstone River in Northbridge and Uxbridge, then follows it through Millville and Blackstone as their main street. In Northbridge, former mills have found new uses as housing and businesses along the river.

The canal’s promoters wanted a different route to market: Providence merchants sought trade with the farming country of the valley and Worcester County. Construction began in 1825, and the waterway opened in 1828. Boats took two days to travel between Worcester and Providence, stopping overnight in Uxbridge. The parallel Providence and Worcester Railroad began operating in 1847; the canal closed the following year.

Traveling south, Grafton’s common gives way to Northbridge and Uxbridge, then Millville and Blackstone at the state line. At the state park in Uxbridge, canal locks and towpaths survive near Goat Hill; Millville has another well-preserved canal lock.

moments.title: Grafton Common
moments.text: Grafton Common’s bandstand began as movie scenery. During the 1930s, a film crew built it on the common; it has since been torn down and rebuilt many times. The bandstand belongs to that film’s legacy, but the structure is not the original movie set. Historic homes, churches and other buildings surround the common.

moments.title: Blackstone River and Canal Heritage State Park
moments.text: A granite lock at Goat Hill gives the Blackstone Canal a physical scale. The canal was a ditch beside the river, with a dirt towpath from which horses pulled the boats. Uxbridge served as the overnight stop on the two-day journey between Worcester and Providence. The park preserves a long canal section, and remnants of locks and towpaths can be seen near Goat Hill. Nearby Lookout Rock offers a view of the valley and the winding Blackstone River.
moments.notice: Near Goat Hill, look for the granite lock and remnants of the canal towpaths.

moments.title: Millville
moments.text: Route 122 follows the Blackstone River through Millville as the town’s main street. A well-preserved lock survives from the Blackstone Canal, whose transportation role passed to the Providence and Worcester Railroad. The canal closed in 1848, long before Millville became a separate town. Incorporated in 1916, Millville had previously been part of Blackstone. The lock therefore belongs to an older geography of the valley, when a waterway linked Worcester’s inland trade with Providence and Narragansett Bay.
